You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failure in X7875_NewUnixTest.testParseReparse() and the production exception reported both point to flaws in X7875_NewUnix.parseFromLocalFileData(byte[], int, int).

What the test exercises
- The test feeds several encoded “ux” extra field payloads into the parser, notably:
  - ZERO_LEN = {1, 0, 0} meaning version=1, uidSize=0, gidSize=0
  - ZERO_UID_GID = {1, 1, 0, 1, 0} meaning version=1, uidSize=1 with value 0, gidSize=1 with value 0
- These cases assert that zero-length and zero-value UID/GID are valid and should parse to 0 without error.

What the code does
- parseFromLocalFileData resets uid/gid to 1000, then parses:
  - version = data[offset++]
  - uidSize = data[offset++]
  - copies uidSize bytes, then sets uid = new BigInteger(1, reverse(uidBytes))
  - gidSize = data[offset++]
  - copies gidSize bytes, then sets gid = new BigInteger(1, reverse(gidBytes))
- Two critical issues here:
  1) Zero-length or zero-value magnitudes:
     - For uidSize == 0 the code constructs new BigInteger(1, new byte[0]).
     - For uidSize == 1 with byte == 0 the magnitude is still zero.
     - According to BigInteger(int signum, byte[] magnitude), signum != 0 with a zero magnitude throws NumberFormatException. This means both ZERO_LEN and ZERO_UID_GID cause a NumberFormatException at uid (and similarly for gid).
     - The test expects these to parse as 0, so the current implementation violates the expected behavior.
  2) No bounds checking against the provided length:
     - The method ignores its length parameter and unconditionally reads at least three bytes (version, uidSize, gidSize) and then copies uidSize and gidSize bytes.
     - If the extra field length is actually 0 (a “0-sized ‘ux’ local entry”), the very first read data[offset++] triggers an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
     - This matches the production bug report reporting ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when Tika processes a ZIP with a zero-sized “ux” extra field.

Additional minor issue
- After copying gidBytes the code doesn’t increment offset by gidSize. This doesn’t cause the current failures (no subsequent reads), but it’s inconsistent and would break if more fields were added later.

How the bug causes the observed failures
- In the test:
  - For ZERO_LEN (3-byte payload), the code reaches new BigInteger(1, new byte[0]) and throws NumberFormatException, failing the test case that expects uid=0, gid=0.
  - For ZERO_UID_GID, constructing BigInteger with a magnitude of all zeros also throws NumberFormatException for both uid and gid.
- In the reported production case:
  - For a truly zero-length “ux” extra field (length == 0), the method reads past the end of data because it ignores the length and immediately dereferences data[offset], causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Root cause
- parseFromLocalFileData lacks:
  - Proper handling of 0-length and zero-valued UID/GID (should assign 0 instead of trying to construct a positive BigInteger with zero magnitude).
  - Any bounds checking using the provided length parameter, leading to out-of-bounds reads when the local extra field size is 0 (or too small).

Consequences
- Tests that include zero-length or zero-valued UID/GID fail with NumberFormatException.
- Real-world ZIPs with an empty “ux” local extra field trigger ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

In short, parseFromLocalFileData needs to:
- Use the length parameter to guard all reads and copies.
- Treat uidSize == 0 (or an all-zero magnitude) as uid = BigInteger.ZERO (and likewise for gid), instead of constructing BigInteger(1, ...).

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
